card.title: Replay your work on top
card.blurb: `git merge` joins two lines of work and records that they met. `git rebase` makes your commits again on top of the other branch, so the history comes out as a straight line. Knowing the difference matters, because a replayed commit is not the commit you had.
hero.title: Replay your work on top
intro.0: You already know one way to bring two branches together. `git merge` joins them and adds a commit that records the meeting. `git rebase` answers the same question differently: it makes your commits again on top of the other branch, and the history comes out as a straight line. The catch is in the word again - the commits you end up with are new ones, with new ids. Here you run a rebase and then go looking for what it left behind.
task.1.title: Put your commit on top of theirs
task.1.context:
While you were working on `feature`, `add dog` landed on `main`. Your branch does not have it yet.

`git rebase <branch>` takes the commits that are on the branch you are standing on and not on `<branch>`, and makes them again on top of it. It works on wherever you happen to be standing, so check that before you run it. `git log` on its own prints a block per commit with the hash on its own line, which reads better than `--oneline` when the hash is the thing you are watching.
task.1.goal.0: Read `git branch`. The `*` marks the branch you are standing on, and it is not the one you have been working on.
task.1.goal.1: Move onto `feature` with `git checkout`. A rebase acts on the branch you are standing on.
task.1.goal.2: Read `git log`. Your branch has two commits and neither of them is `add dog`. Note the hash on `add bird`.
task.1.goal.3: Replay your work on top of `main` with one `git rebase`.
task.1.goal.4: Read `git log --oneline`. Three commits in one line now, and the hash on `add bird` is not the one you noted.
task.2.title: The commit you started with is still there
task.2.context:
The rebase has already happened here. `feature` is one straight line on top of `main`, and the `add bird` sitting on it is a commit that did not exist a moment ago.

The one you had before is still in the repository. Nothing points at it, so `git log` cannot reach it - but `git reflog` lists every place `HEAD` has stood, and the old commit is on that list with its own hash. Put a branch on it and both versions are on the board at once.
task.2.goal.0: Read `git log`. Three commits in one line, and `add bird` sits on `add dog`. Note the hash it has now.
task.2.goal.1: Read `git reflog`. The line that says `commit: add bird` is the commit from before the replay, and it starts with a different hash.
task.2.goal.2: Put a branch called `before-rebase` on it with `git branch before-rebase <hash>`.
task.2.goal.3: Move onto it with `git checkout before-rebase`.
task.2.goal.4: Read `git log --oneline`. `add bird` on `add cat`, and no `add dog` - the line you had before the rebase, still there to walk.
task.3.title: Replay your work on top - recap
task.3.context: Two ways to bring work together, two shapes of history.
task.3.summaryIntro: `git merge` and `git rebase` answer the same question and leave different histories behind. A merge keeps both lines and adds a commit that joins them, so the history records what actually happened. A rebase makes your commits again on top of the other branch, so the history reads as though you had started later. Remaking the commits is the part worth thinking about: the originals stay in the repository with nothing pointing at them, and anyone who already has them is left holding work you no longer have under those ids.
task.3.summaryItems.0.title: `git rebase <branch>` -
task.3.summaryItems.0.text: takes the commits on the branch you are standing on that `<branch>` cannot reach, and makes them again on top of it.
task.3.summaryItems.1.title: A replayed commit -
task.3.summaryItems.1.text: keeps its message and gets a new parent, which gives it a new id. The commit you started with stays in the repository with nothing pointing at it.
task.3.summaryItems.2.title: `git reflog` -
task.3.summaryItems.2.text: still lists the commits from before the replay, so a branch on one of those hashes brings the old line back.
task.3.summaryItems.3.title: Merge or rebase -
task.3.summaryItems.3.text: merge when the join is worth recording, rebase when you want one straight line. Work that someone else already has is the case to leave alone: replaying it hands them a second copy of the same commits.
task.3.summaryClose: That closes the git track. You have both ways of bringing two lines of work together now, and a reason to pick one.
concept.gt-rebase.def: Making the commits on your branch again on top of another branch, which leaves the history as one straight line and gives every replayed commit a new id.
